quick.summary: How to keep track of a single customer across many conflicting systems.
quick.takeaway: Connect systems using a shared identity and an event hub to stay in sync.

parts.title: Syncing multiple systems

beats.line: Every team has a different list of customers. How do we count them all?
Imagine ordering food. The kitchen calls you table four. The driver calls you Dave.
Same person, different labels. Systems do this too. Billing uses an account number.
Support uses an email address. They do not match.
So how do we know Dave is table four?
We need a central record. A single source of truth for each person.
The industry calls this master data management.
Can I just say one shared identity?
But every system changes their data every day. How do we keep up?

parts.cliff: How to keep systems in sync without manual work.

beats.line: We stop passing files around and start publishing events.
Think of a town square. When someone moves, they shout it out once.
Anyone who cares writes it down. Anyone who does not care ignores it.
So when a customer updates their address, billing shouts it out?
Yes. And shipping hears it and updates their own list immediately.
We use a central hub to pass the message to everyone.
So shipping and billing stay in sync without talking directly?
You got it. And your customer list finally matches everywhere.

quiz.question: Why is it hard to count customers across multiple systems?
options: Each system identifies the same person differently.
The databases are too small to hold everyone.
Customers forget their passwords too often.
The business does not care about total counts.
quiz.explanation: Different systems track users by different labels, making it impossible to get a true count without linking them.

quiz.question: To keep systems in sync, every system should connect directly to every other system.
quiz.explanation: Connecting systems directly creates a mess. It is better to use a central event hub where systems broadcast and listen for changes.
